claim: Cancer cells display high levels of oncogene-induced replication stress (RS) and rely on DNA damage checkpoint for viability.
source: Cancer cells display high levels of oncogene-induced replication stress (RS) and rely on DNA damage checkpoint for viability.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding about cancer cell biology.

claim: Bakuchiol inhibited DNA replication and activated the checkpoint kinase CHK1 by targeting DNA polymerases.
source: Bakuchiol inhibited DNA replication and activated the checkpoint kinase CHK1 by targeting DNA polymerases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including DNA fiber assays, western blots, and molecular docking studies.

claim: Isobavachalcone interfered with DNA double-strand break repair by inhibiting the checkpoint kinase CHK2 and DNA end resection.
source: Isobavachalcone interfered with DNA double-strand break repair by inhibiting the checkpoint kinase CHK2 and DNA end resection.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assays, SMART assays, and RAD51 foci formation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The combination of bakuchiol and isobavachalcone synergistically inhibited cancer cell proliferation in vitro.
source: The combination of bakuchiol and isobavachalcone synergistically inhibited cancer cell proliferation in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by concentration matrix analyses and cell viability assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: The combination of bakuchiol and isobavachalcone prevented tumor development in xenografted NOD/SCID mice.
source: Importantly, it also prevented tumor development in xenografted NOD/SCID mice.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft experiments measuring tumor size and survival rates shown in Figure 6.

claim: Faithful DNA replication depends on the coordinated action of the many enzymes that make up the replisome.
source: Faithful DNA replication depends on the coordinated action of the many enzymes that make up the replisome (Attali et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DNA is synthesized on the leading strand by DNA polymerase (Pol) ε and on the lagging strand by Pol α-primase and Pol δ.
source: DNA is synthesized on the leading strand by DNA polymerase (Pol) ε and on the lagging strand by Pol α-primase and Pol δ (Lujan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA replication supported by a citation.

claim: Replication forks stall when they encounter obstacles such as DNA lesions, highly transcribed genes, or tightly bound protein complexes, causing replication stress.
source: Replication forks stall when they encounter obstacles such as DNA lesions, highly transcribed genes, or tightly bound protein complexes, causing what is commonly referred to as replication stress (RS) (Lin and Pasero, 2021; Macheret and Halazonetis, 2015; Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about replication stress supported by multiple citations.

claim: RS is associated with an excess of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), resulting from the uncoupling of DNA polymerase and helicase activities.
source: RS is associated with an excess of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), resulting from the uncoupling of DNA polymerase and helicase activities (Pasero and Vindigni, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK phosphorylate the histone variant H2AX on S139 (γ-H2AX), which is a reliable biomarker of RS and DSBs.
source: ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK phosphorylate the histone variant H2AX on S139 (γ-H2AX), which is a reliable biomarker of RS and DSBs (Bonner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: During the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, DSBs are preferentially repaired by homologous recombination (HR), which uses the sister chromatid as repair template.
source: During the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, DSBs are preferentially repaired by homologous recombination (HR), which uses the sister chromatid as repair template (Moynahan and Jasin, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA repair supported by a citation.

claim: BKC and IBC were identified from an extract prepared from Psoralea corylifolia.
source: In an extract prepared from P. corylifolia, we identified two compounds, IBC (MW: 324.4; Kuete and Sandjo, 2012) and BKC (MW: 256.4; Nizam et al., 2023; Figure 1A)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IBC and BKC inhibited the proliferation of MCF-7 cells and A549 human lung cancer cells more than they did the proliferation of BJ fibroblasts and non-transformed epithelial cells MCF10A and RPE-1 cells.
source: which inhibited the proliferation of MCF-7 cells and A549 human lung cancer cells more than they did the proliferation of BJ fibroblasts and non-transformed epithelial cells MCF10A and RPE-1 cells (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assays shown in the referenced figures.

claim: BKC is a bioactive meroterpene that possesses a variety of pharmacological activities.
source: BKC is a bioactive meroterpene that possesses a variety of pharmacological activities (Xin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BKC was shown to inhibit the proliferation of many cancer cell lines presumably through the inhibition of DNA replication.
source: It was shown to inhibit the proliferation of many cancer cell lines (Li et al., 2016) presumably through the inhibition of DNA replication (Sun et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: IBC is a natural chalcone that exhibits potential anticancer activities.
source: IBC is a natural chalcone that also exhibits potential anticancer activities (Kuete et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In all cell lines tested, a synergistic effect of IBC and BKC was observed over a narrow range of concentrations (3–10 µM IBC and 10–30 µM BKC).
source: In all cell lines tested, we observed a synergistic effect of IBC and BKC over a narrow range of concentrations (3–10 µM IBC and 10–30 µM BKC)
evidence: This is supported by concentration matrix analyses shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ratio of 3:10 µM IBC:BKC that has a synergistic effect in vitro corresponds to the ratio of concentrations of the two compounds in the fruits of P. corylifolia.
source: This ratio of 3:10 µM IBC:BKC that has a synergistic effect in vitro corresponds to the ratio of concentrations of the two compounds in the fruits of P. corylifolia.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing in vitro concentrations to natural concentrations.

claim: IBC increased γ-H2AX signal in MCF-7 but not in BJ cells.
source: IBC increased γ-H2AX signal in MCF-7 but not in BJ cells
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: BKC increased γ-H2AX signal in both MCF-7 and BJ cell types.
source: whereas BKC increased it in both cell types (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The combination of IBC and BKC further increased γ-H2AX fluorescence in MCF-7 but not in BJ cells.
source: Moreover, the combination of IBC and BKC further increased γ-H2AX fluorescence in MCF-7 but not in BJ cells (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: BKC alone or in combination with IBC induced phosphorylation of CHK1 on S345 in MCF-7 cells, whereas IBC alone did not.
source: BKC alone or in combination with IBC also induced phosphorylation of CHK1 on S345 in MCF-7 cells, whereas IBC alone did not (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: BKC reduced fork speed by a factor of two relative to untreated cells in both MCF-7 and BJ cell lines.
source: Analysis of CldU track length showed that BKC reduced fork speed by a factor of two relative to untreated cells in both cell lines
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber spreading assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: IBC inhibited fork speed more in MCF-7 cells than in BJ cells.
source: In contrast, IBC inhibited fork speed more in MCF-7 cells than in BJ cells
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber spreading assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment with BKC, but not IBC, resulted in a greater proportion of both cell types in S phase.
source: Treatment with BKC, but not IBC, resulted in a greater proportion of both cell types in S phase
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BKC inhibited fork progression in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Using DNA fiber assay, we found that BKC inhibited fork progression in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: BKC treatment significantly increased sister fork asymmetry compared to DMSO-treated control cells.
source: Furthermore, BKC treatment significantly increased sister fork asymmetry compared to DMSO-treated control cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: BKC inhibited fork progression more effectively than aphidicolin at the tested concentrations.
source: Remarkably, BKC inhibited fork progression more effectively than aphidicolin at these concentrations
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber spreading data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The combined effect of BKC and aphidicolin was similar to the effect of BKC alone.
source: and the combined effect of both compounds was similar to the effect of BKC alone (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber spreading data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When added at the start of the Xenopus egg extract assay (0 min), BKC (100 µM) exhibited a strong inhibitory effect on DNA replication, although not as profound as the effect of aphidicolin (60 µM).
source: When added at the start of the assay (0 min), BKC (100 µM) exhibited a strong inhibitory effect on DNA replication, although not as profound as the effect of aphidicolin (60 µM).
evidence: This is supported by DNA replication assay data in Xenopus egg extracts shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When added after 40 min, BKC was as effective as aphidicolin in inhibiting DNA replication in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Moreover, when added after 40 min, long after the initiation of replication, BKC was as effective as aphidicolin (Figure 2H)
evidence: This is supported by DNA replication assay data in Xenopus egg extracts shown in Figure 2H.

claim: BKC effectively inhibited replication of ssDNA in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Consistent with this possibility, BKC effectively inhibited replication of ssDNA, a process that relies entirely on priming and elongation of DNA chains by replicative DNA polymerases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ssDNA replication assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In silico molecular docking showed that BKC can occupy the deoxycytidine sites of both DNA polymerases δ and ε.
source: This analysis showed that BKC can occupy the deoxycytidine sites of both enzymes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by in silico molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: BKC interacts with the catalytic subunits of Polδ and Polε in MCF-7 cells to stabilize the thermal sensitivity of both proteins.
source: Using the cellular thermal sensitivity shift assay (CETSA) (Martinez Molina et al., 2013), we found that BKC interacts with the catalytic subunits of Polδ and Polε in MCF-7 cells to stabilize the thermal sensitivity of both proteins (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by CETSA data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: BKC specifically stabilizes the catalytic subunit POLD1 of Polδ, but not the accessory subunit POLD3 in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Importantly, BKC specifically stabilize the catalytic subunit POLD1 of Polδ, but not that of the accessory subunit POLD3 in Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by CETSA data in Xenopus egg extracts shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: BKC did not alter the thermal sensitivity of Xenopus PCNA.
source: Similarly, BKC did not alter the thermal sensitivity of Xenopus PCNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by CETSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At the concentrations used in this study, IBC inhibition of DNA replication cannot be explained by inhibition of AKT.
source: We conclude that, at the concentrations used in this study, IBC inhibition of DNA replication cannot be explained by inhibition of AKT.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experiments showing IBC does not inhibit AKT phosphorylation or affect AKT-regulated genes at the concentrations used.

claim: The most sensitive kinase to IBC, CHK2, had an IC50 of 3.5 µM.
source: The most sensitive kinase, CHK2, had an IC50 for IBC of 3.5 µM (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Aurora-A/B and JNK3 were sensitive to IBC at approximately fivefold higher concentrations than CHK2.
source: Aurora-A/B and JNK3 were also sensitive to IBC, but at approximately fivefold higher concentrations, IC50 of 11.2 µM for Aurora-A/B and 16.4 µM for JNK3.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CHK1 was not inhibited by IBC.
source: By contrast, CHK1 was not inhibited by IBC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The IC50 of IBC for AKT1/PKBα was 56.7 µM.
source: Consistent with our findings above, the IC50 for AKT1/PKBα was 56.7 µM (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: IBC inhibited the autophosphorylation of CHK2 on S516 induced by CPT by approximately 50%.
source: In MCF-7 cells, IBC inhibited the autophosphorylation of CHK2 induced by CPT by approximately 50% (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: IBC reduced the phosphorylation of chromatin-bound BRCA1 at residue S988 induced by CPT, as efficiently as the commercial CHK2 inhibitor BML-277.
source: We showed that treatment with IBC reduced the phosphorylation of chromatin-bound BRCA1 at residue S988 induced by CPT, as efficiently as the commercial CHK2 inhibitor BML-277 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: IBC did not affect the autophosphorylation of CHK1 on S296 induced by hydroxyurea.
source: By contrast, IBC did not affect the autophosphorylation of CHK1 on S296 induced by hydroxyurea (HU; Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: IBC binds to the active site of CHK2 by means of a hydrogen bond and 11 hydrophobic interactions.
source: Using in silico molecular docking, we found that IBC binds to the active site of CHK2 by means of a hydrogen bond and 11 hydrophobic interactions (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is supported by in silico molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: IBC binding to the active site of CHK1 is prevented by a steric clash with a tyrosine residue (Tyr86).
source: whereas its binding to the active site of CHK1 is prevented by a steric clash with a tyrosine residue (Tyr86) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by in silico molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: IBC altered the thermal stability of CHK2 as efficiently as the commercial CHK2 inhibitor, BML-277, without affecting the thermal stability of CHK1.
source: We showed that IBC altered the thermal stability of CHK2 as efficiently as the commercial CHK2 inhibitor, BML-277, without affecting the thermal stability of CHK1 (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by CETSA data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: In cells treated with IBC, the CPT-induced 53BP1 foci persisted.
source: In cells treated with IBC, the CPT-induced 53BP1 foci persisted
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In cells not treated with IBC, the intensity of the CPT-induced 53BP1 immunofluorescence signal increased and returned to basal levels 24 hr later.
source: whereas in cells not treated with IBC, the intensity of the CPT-induced 53BP1 immunofluorescence signal increased and returned to basal levels 24 hr later (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: IBC inhibited the formation of RPA-coated ssDNA upon CPT treatment.
source: These analyses revealed that IBC inhibited the formation of RPA-coated ssDNA upon CPT treatment (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: BrdU tracks were significantly shorter when CHK2 was inhibited either by IBC or by the CHK2 inhibitor BML-277.
source: We found that the BrdU tracks were significantly shorter when CHK2 was inhibited either by IBC or by the CHK2 inhibitor BML-277 (Arienti et al., 2005; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by SMART assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: IBC impaired DNA end resection induced by gamma irradiation.
source: Using the same assay, we found that IBC also impaired DNA end resection induced by gamma irradiation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by SMART assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: IBC inhibited the formation of ssDNA at two break sites induced by AsiSI digestion.
source: IBC inhibited the formation of ssDNA at two break sites induced by AsiSI digestion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5F)
evidence: This is supported by DIvA system data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: CHK2 inhibition by either IBC or BML-277 completely prevented formation of RAD51 foci in response to ionizing radiation.
source: CHK2 inhibition by either IBC or BML-277 completely prevented formation of RAD51 foci in response to ionizing radiation (Figure 5G)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: IBC completely prevented formation of RAD51 foci in response to bleomycin.
source: and IBC completely prevented formation of RAD51 foci in response to bleomycin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: After 3 weeks, IBC and BKC significantly inhibited tumor growth in a dose-dependent manner in xenografted mice.
source: After 3 weeks, IBC and BKC significantly inhibited tumor growth in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: IBC had a stronger effect on the growth of MCF-7/Luc cells than BKC had in xenografted mice.
source: IBC had a stronger effect on the growth of MCF-7/Luc cells than BKC had
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The combined use of IBC and BKC had the greatest inhibitory effect on tumor growth in xenografted mice.
source: but the combined use of both compounds had the greatest inhibitory effect on tumor growth (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The mice injected with the higher dose of IBC or of the IBC + BKC combination survived longer than those treated with Taxol.
source: Moreover, the mice injected with the higher dose of IBC or of the IBC + BKC combination survived longer than those treated with Taxol (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by survival data from xenograft experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: IBC and BKC inhibited tumor cell proliferation in xenografted mice.
source: Overall, IBC and BKC inhibited tumor cell proliferation (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 immunohistochemistry data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: IBC and BKC induced DNA fragmentation, indicative of tumor cell death by apoptosis in xenografted mice.
source: and induced DNA fragmentation, indicative of tumor cell death by apoptosis (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The percentage of TUNEL-positive cells was much higher in mice treated with IBC + BKC5x than either drug alone.
source: However, the percentage of TUNEL-positive cells was much higher in mice treated with IBC + BKC5x than either drug alone (Figure 6E)
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A dose-dependent increase in CHK1 phosphorylation was observed in tumor tissues from mice treated with BKC.
source: We also observed a dose-dependent increase in CHK1 phosphorylation in tumor tissues from mice treated with BKC (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: BKC induced phosphorylation of CHK2 on T68, a marker of DNA damage, in tumor tissues.
source: Moreover, BKC induced phosphorylation of CHK2 on T68, a marker of DNA damage (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The activation of CHK1 and CHK2 mediated by BKC was suppressed by the addition of IBC in tumor tissues.
source: However, this activation of CHK1 and CHK2 mediated by BKC was suppressed by the addition of IBC (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Treatment with the higher concentration of IBC alone diminished the level of endogenous phosphorylation of both CHK1 and CHK2 in tumor tissues.
source: Interestingly, treatment with the higher concentration of IBC alone diminished the level of endogenous phosphorylation of both CHK1 and CHK2
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: IC50 of IBC for growth inhibition of DLBCL cell lines ranged from 8 to 28 μM.
source: IC50 ranged from 8 to 28 μM (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: IBC substantially enhanced cell growth inhibition by etoposide, doxorubicin, and 4-hydroxy-cyclophosphamide in U2932 DLBCL cells.
source: We found that IBC substantially enhanced cell growth inhibition by all three of these DNA-damaging agents (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: IBC synergistically increased the inhibitory effect of doxorubicin and 4-hydroxy-cyclophosphamide on U2932 cell proliferation.
source: Moreover, by testing a full-range concentration matrix of drug pairs on cell viability after 72 hr treatment, we found that IBC synergistically increased the inhibitory effect of doxorubicin and or 4-hydroxy-cyclophosphamide on U2932 cell proliferation (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by concentration matrix analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: BKC probably inhibits DNA polymerases by competing for dNTP binding.
source: This is consistent with our evidence from in silico molecular docking that BKC binds the catalytic site of DNA polymerases δ and ε. Thus, BKC probably inhibits the polymerases by competing for dNTP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular docking data showing BKC binds to the dNTP binding site.

claim: BKC acts as a bona fide replication inhibitor.
source: Moreover, we show that BKC slows replication fork progression in vivo in both normal and cancer cells, indicating that it acts as a bona fide replication inhibitor.
evidence: This conclusion is based on DNA fiber assay data showing BKC slows fork progression.

claim: The target of IBC in vivo is very likely CHK2-dependent activation of BRCA1.
source: The target of IBC in vivo is very likely CHK2-dependent activation of BRCA1.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing IBC inhibits CHK2 and prevents BRCA1 phosphorylation.

claim: IBC does not inhibit resection of nascent DNA at stalled forks.
source: In contrast, IBC does not inhibit resection of nascent DNA at stalled forks, a process that does not depend on BRCA1 but, rather, is repressed by BRCA1 and BRCA2 (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on the known role of BRCA1/2 in protecting stalled forks and the specificity of IBC for CHK2-BRCA1 pathway.

claim: IBC differentially affects resection at DSB and at stalled forks by inhibiting CHK2.
source: Our data indicate therefore that IBC differentially affects resection at DSB and at stalled forks by inhibiting CHK2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing IBC inhibits resection at DSBs but not at stalled forks.

claim: BKC increases replication stress in cancer cells by inhibiting bulk DNA synthesis, increasing the rate of replication fork arrest/collapse and inducing RS-dependent DSBs.
source: The inhibitory effects of BKC on DNA synthesis and IBC on DNA end resection support a model in which BKC increases RS in cancer cells by inhibiting bulk DNA synthesis, so increasing the rate of replication fork arrest/collapse and inducing RS-dependent DSBs
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings about BKC's effects on DNA replication.

claim: IBC inhibits HR-mediated DSB repair, resulting in cell death by apoptosis.
source: and IBC inhibits HR-mediated DSB repair, resulting in cell death by apoptosis (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data showing IBC prevents RAD51 foci formation and increases apoptosis.

claim: BKC-mediated RS adds to oncogene-induced RS, explaining the differential sensitivity of normal and cancer cells to the combination of BKC and IBC.
source: This model explains why BKC and IBC synergistically inhibit the proliferation of cancer cells: BKC-mediated RS adds to oncogene-induced RS, explaining the differential sensitivity of normal and cancer cells to the combination of BKC and IBC, and also to the effects of IBC alone.
evidence: This is an explanation proposed to account for the observed synergistic effects and differential sensitivity.

claim: IBC or other clinically approved CHK2 inhibitors could be used to potentiate the cytotoxic effect of known DNA damaging agents.
source: Although it is unlikely that these compounds will ever be used in combination therapies, our results indicate that IBC or other clinically approved CHK2 inhibitors could be used to potentiate the cytotoxic effect of known DNA damaging agents.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results showing IBC potentiates chemotherapeutic agents.

claim: RS and DNA damage stimulate anti-tumor immunity by activating cytosolic nucleic acid-sensing pathways.
source: Finally, recent evidence indicates that RS and DNA damage stimulate anti-tumor immunity by activating cytosolic nucleic acid-sensing pathways (Chabanon et al., 2021; Tarsounas and Sung, 2020; Técher and Pasero, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: New combinations of genotoxic agents and inhibitors targeting RS checkpoint kinases might be valuable for potentiating immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: New combinations of genotoxic agents and inhibitors targeting RS checkpoint kinases might thus be valuable also for potentiating immune checkpoint inhibitors.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on recent findings about RS and immunity.
